issues.description: The central construct is framed as spelling-to-meaning regularity, but the operational outcome is lexical category (noun/adjective/verb), which is primarily syntactic/grammatical rather than semantic meaning. This mismatch matters because the behavioral tasks may show sensitivity to grammatical category cues without demonstrating sensitivity to meaning, semantic interpretation, or morphology-to-semantics mappings. Claims about "meaningful information" and "access to meaning" are therefore broader than what was measured.
issues.quote: This paper focuses on one aspect of word meaning, specifically, lexical category (e.g., noun, adjective, verb; see Baayen et al., 2011, for a similar conceptualisation of “meaning”).

issues.description: The stated type-diagnosticity formula contradicts the construct definition. Diagnosticity is described as how well a suffix spelling predicts lexical category, i.e. P(category | suffix). But the manuscript says it divides by the total number of words in the category, which is P(suffix | category). This is the opposite conditional probability and overlaps conceptually with specificity. The examples and token formula appear to use a different denominator, creating a serious reproducibility and interpretation problem for the central measure.
issues.quote: We define diagnosticity as the strength with which a suffix spelling predicts lexical category.  For a particular suffix, type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.

issues.description: The stated token-specificity denominator is inconsistent with the definition of specificity as P(spelling | sound sequence, category). The denominator should include all words of the relevant category with the relevant sound sequence, across all spellings. Instead, the text says the denominator is all words that contain the target spelling and fall into the category, which would not compare competing spellings and could make the numerator and denominator nearly identical. This makes the token-specificity estimates non-replicable from the description.
issues.quote: A second measure of specificity, based on word tokens, was obtained by dividing the summed frequency of words ending in this phonological and orthographic sequence and falling into this category by the summed frequency of all words that contain the spelling and fall into this category.

issues.description: Diagnosticity and specificity are category-specific quantities, and Appendix A reports separate values for adjectives, nouns, and verbs. However, the main analyses report a single diagnosticity and specificity value per suffix, without explaining whether this is the maximum across categories, the value for the suffix's dominant category, an average, or something else. This omission affects interpretation of Figure 2, stimulus selection, correlations, and all graded behavioral analyses.
issues.quote: Our analyses consider three major lexical categories: nouns, adjectives, and verbs. Only the most frequent pronunciation was considered for each suffix. ... Mean type diagnosticity for suffixes is 0.78 (token – 0.77), mean specificity is 0.82 (token – 0.83).

issues.subcategory: excluded lexical categories affect construct estimates
issues.description: The analyses restrict lexical category to nouns, adjectives, and verbs even though many suffixes cue other categories such as adverbs, numerals, or function-word classes. The authors later acknowledge that some low values arise because relevant categories were not considered. This means diagnosticity/specificity values are not general measures of lexical-category information, and some suffixes may be mischaracterized as nondiagnostic merely because their true category was excluded.
issues.quote: Preliminary analyses we conducted to understanding why some morphemes are diagnostic, while others are not. For this analysis, we removed seven suffixes with diagnosticity below 0.35, because these are indicative of lexical categories we have not considered in this paper (e.g. –WISE, –TEEN).

issues.description: The manuscript reports 154 suffixes, then states that 64 were excluded for occurring in fewer than 20 words, leaving 95 suffixes. This arithmetic is impossible: 154 minus 64 equals 90, not 95. Because these counts determine the corpus subset used to support the claim that high diagnosticity/specificity is not driven by rare suffixes, the inconsistency undermines confidence in the reported corpus analysis.
issues.quote: This process revealed 154 written suffixes in total. ... In order to determine this, we excluded all suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 different words in the CELEX database, i.e. 64 suffixes (Baayen et al., 1993).  For the remaining 95 suffixes, the mean diagnosticity and specificity values were virtually unchanged

issues.description: The methods state that suffixes were included only if they occurred in at least three different words, yet Appendix A includes multiple suffixes with type frequencies of 1 or 2. This contradicts the stated extraction rule and makes the computational sample ambiguous.
issues.quote: Using this list of words as our database, we extracted all spellings annotated as derivational suffixes in CELEX that occur in at least three different words. ... 34 | +efy | ... | Type frequency | 1

issues.subcategory: CELEX sample overgeneralized to all English suffixes
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly claims to characterize all English derivational suffixes, but the analysis is limited to CELEX single-word entries, CELEX morphological annotations, exclusions of hyphenated/spaced forms, and only suffixes satisfying the authors' extraction criteria. CELEX is a finite lexical database with known coverage and annotation limitations, so the claim should be restricted to the analyzed corpus sample.
issues.quote: In this paper, we present a computational analysis that characterizes the relationship between spelling and lexical category across all derivational suffixes in English. ... We extracted all single-word entries from the CELEX database (Baayen, Piepenbrock & van Rijn, 1993), excluding any entries with spaces or hyphens.

issues.description: Specificity depends on the mapping from a suffix spelling to its sound sequence, but the analysis uses only the most frequent pronunciation of each suffix. Many English suffixes and final spellings have multiple pronunciations depending on stress, base, dialect, and lexical item. Ignoring pronunciation variability may misestimate specificity, especially for suffixes such as -ate, -er, -al, -y, and -ise/-ize, and limits dialectal generalizability.
issues.quote: Only the most frequent pronunciation was considered for each suffix. ... In order to calculate specificity, we identified the most frequent pronunciation of each suffix

issues.description: The corpus analysis depends on identifying words containing genuine suffixes and pseudo-suffixes, but the algorithm for determining a "legitimate stem" and allowable orthographic alternations is not fully specified. The example COMPLI- suggests nontrivial manual or rule-based decisions. Without a reproducible description of the alternation inventory, stem criteria, and handling of overlapping suffixes, the corpus counts cannot be independently evaluated.
issues.quote: we extracted all words containing the spelling of each suffix, as long as the remaining (non-suffix) portion comprised a legitimate stem with at least one phonological vowel in the CELEX database (including stems with alternations i.e. orthographically conditioned variations, such as COMPLI-).

issues.description: The computational-analysis conclusion reverses the logical mapping between diagnosticity/specificity and the behavioral tasks. Diagnosticity is defined as spelling-to-category and should predict print-to-category tasks; specificity is defined as category/sound-to-spelling and should predict spelling production. The manuscript states the opposite in one paragraph, then gives the correct predictions in the Experiments section. This creates conceptual confusion about the theoretical framework.
issues.quote: we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the production of spelling, while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning ... We predicted that in tasks requiring access to grammatical information from printed spellings (lexical category judgment and sentence reading), spellings with higher diagnosticity should yield stronger behavioural effects ... in tasks requiring production of spellings associated with a particular lexical category, stronger behavioural effects would be observed for those spellings with higher specificity.

issues.description: The participants are described only as Royal Holloway undergraduates. No age range, gender distribution, native-language criteria, dialect background, literacy level, spelling ability, reading ability, exclusion criteria, or vision status are reported. Because the manuscript makes claims about skilled readers and spelling knowledge, these omissions limit interpretability and replicability.
issues.quote: Participants were 46 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway, University of London. ... Participants were 29 undergraduate students from Royal Holloway University of London. ... 47 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway University of London were recruited following the same procedure as in Experiments 1 and 2.

issues.subcategory: no power analysis and small suffix-level samples
issues.description: No a priori power analysis or precision justification is reported. Although the trial counts are moderate, the theoretically relevant units are suffixes: Experiment 1 has 20 suffixes, Experiment 2 has 11 target spellings, and Experiment 3 has 20 analyzed noun/adjective suffixes. Graded diagnosticity/specificity analyses and interactions at the suffix level are therefore likely underpowered and sensitive to individual suffixes.
issues.quote: Twenty suffixes diagnostic for the noun or adjective category were selected ... Eleven suffix spellings that had a high specificity for noun, adjective, or verb lexical category were selected. ... Eighty experimental nonwords with suffix spellings diagnostic for adjectives (10 suffixes) or nouns (10 suffixes) were selected from Experiment 1.

issues.description: Experiments 1 and 2 analyze repeated observations with only a subject random intercept and no item or suffix random effects, despite the manipulation being carried by suffixes/items. Experiment 3 includes subject and suffix intercepts but no item intercepts or random slopes. This treats item/suffix variability as fixed or ignores it, inflates degrees of freedom, and can produce anti-conservative p-values for the core effects.
issues.quote: We included a random intercept for subjects. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial"). ... The analyses were otherwise identical to those in Experiment 1. ... All models included trial order as a main effect, and random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes.

issues.description: Suffixes selected for adjective and noun conditions differ in many properties besides diagnosticity, including length, type frequency, token frequency, productivity, orthographic neighborhood, morphological transparency, and familiarity. These variables are not matched or included as covariates in the behavioral models. Thus graded diagnosticity effects may partially reflect uncontrolled suffix-level confounds.
issues.quote: Twenty suffixes diagnostic for the noun or adjective category were selected (See Table 2).  These suffixes all had a high diagnosticity, i.e. greater than or equal to 0.50, and occurred in at least 20 different words.

issues.description: Experiment 1 excluded 11.7% of trials because of timeouts or invalid button presses, but missingness is not reported by condition, suffix, participant, or item. Because the task imposed a two-second timeout despite instructions not emphasizing speed, missingness may index difficulty and could be systematically related to diagnosticity or category. Excluding these observations without analysis may bias the results.
issues.quote: Instructions did not emphasise speed, although participants needed to make their decisions within a two-second timeout period. ... 1,625 data points (11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response).

issues.description: The Experiment 1 graded analysis multiplies diagnosticity by -1 for noun suffixes to create a single signed predictor. This transformation embeds the expected direction into the predictor and combines category contrast with diagnosticity magnitude. The separate adjective/noun analyses then rely on only 10 suffixes per group and still lack suffix random effects. The analysis should have been pre-specified and modeled with appropriate suffix-level uncertainty.
issues.quote: In order to investigate this statistically, we multiplied our diagnosticity measure by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes and substituted this measure in our model, in place of the condition variable.

issues.subcategory: no behavioral control for nonmorphological orthographic cues
issues.description: The experiments do not include matched nonmorphological endings or phonological controls, so they cannot isolate whether behavior reflects morphological suffix knowledge specifically rather than broader orthographic, phonotactic, or distributional cues at word endings. The authors explicitly state that Experiment 1 was not designed to adjudicate between orthographic and morphological cues, but later conclusions emphasize morphology and spelling-to-meaning regularities.
issues.quote: We did not include non-pseudoaffixed words because the goal of this experiment was not to adjudicate between types of cues used in lexical category judgement (e.g. orthographic vs morphological).

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 stems not crossed with context
issues.description: In Experiment 2, different nonword stems appear in congruent and incongruent contexts for a given suffix. Therefore context effects can be confounded with stem phonotactics, acoustic realization, ease of spelling, sentence frame, or item-specific properties. The claim that no matching was required because the same phonological sequence was used ignores the fact that the whole nonword and sentence differed across conditions.
issues.quote: Stems were joined with suffixes at random; one suffix was used with six different stems. ... Each participant heard six nonwords containing each suffix: three times in a context congruent with the target spelling of the suffix, and three times in a context incongruent with it.

issues.subcategory: sentence contexts not always valid category manipulations
issues.description: The manuscript claims that verb contexts followed an adverb, but some Appendix C items labeled as verb contexts do not follow this template and instead use constructions such as "seemed ___ by", which may cue adjectival/passive participial interpretations rather than verbs. This weakens the manipulation of lexical category in Experiment 2.
issues.quote: Nonwords in verb contexts followed an adverb. ... The glistening water seemed <___> by the colourful lights. | verb | INC | tɒzlət

issues.subcategory: manual spelling coding lacks reliability information
issues.description: Experiment 2 relies on manual extraction and classification of suffix spellings, but the manuscript does not report coding rules, coder blinding, number of coders, inter-rater reliability, or how ambiguous spellings were handled. This is important because typed nonword spellings can be variable and suffix boundaries may be ambiguous.
issues.quote: Suffix spellings were manually extracted from whole nonword spellings (1,914 analysable data points).

issues.subcategory: binary target-spelling outcome loses category-relevant alternatives
issues.description: The Experiment 2 dependent variable codes only whether the participant used the predesignated target spelling, not whether the produced spelling was category-appropriate or predicted by competing spellings of the same sound sequence. This can obscure theoretically relevant responses and makes the interpretation of "other spelling" heterogeneous.
issues.quote: The dependent variable was binary and coded whether the actual spelling was the target spelling for this suffix or not

issues.description: The reported token-specificity interaction in Experiment 2 gives z = 0.60 with p < 0.01. A z value of 0.60 corresponds to a two-sided p value around .55, not < .01. This is a clear statistical reporting error and calls into question the token-based result.
issues.quote: for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01

issues.description: The number of words before the target differed significantly across congruent and incongruent conditions. Pretarget context length and target position can influence eye movements, predictability, parafoveal processing, and regression behavior. The manuscript acknowledges the difference but does not report controlling it in the models.
issues.quote: Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05).

issues.description: The sentence-reading and spelling experiments depend on context congruency, but the manuscript does not report norming for plausibility, predictability, naturalness, cloze probability, syntactic bias strength, or semantic anomaly. Eye-movement differences in Experiment 3 could therefore reflect sentence-level difficulty rather than suffix-category conflict.
issues.quote: One hundred and twenty sentences were designed following noun, adjective, and verb sentence templates used in Experiment 2

issues.description: Experiment 3 explicitly had no concrete prediction about which eye-movement measures would show effects, then tested multiple dependent variables and additional interactions. No correction for multiple testing, preregistered outcome hierarchy, or confirmatory/exploratory distinction is reported. This increases the risk of false positives.
issues.quote: We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation, so we chose to monitor a variety of typically studied measures

issues.subcategory: post hoc graded analyses only on significant eye measures
issues.description: The graded diagnosticity analyses in Experiment 3 were conducted only for the two measures that first showed congruency effects, rather than across all predefined measures or within a preregistered model. This selective follow-up can capitalize on chance and overstate the robustness of diagnosticity modulation.
issues.quote: Further analyses investigated whether the size of the congruency effects on the go-past and regressions-out measures was influenced by the degree to which suffix spellings were diagnostic of lexical category.

issues.subcategory: incomplete reporting of discarded eye-tracking data
issues.description: The eye-tracking procedure discarded trials when calibration/triggering failed and after visual inspection, but the number of gaze-trigger failures is not reported, and the 4% discarded trials are not broken down by condition, participant, item, or reason. If exclusions differ by congruency or target difficulty, the eye-movement effects could be biased.
issues.quote: If a participant failed to do this, the trial was ended and discarded from further analysis, and the calibration procedure was repeated before the next trial was presented. ... As a result of these checks, 4% of trials were discarded.

issues.description: The reported comprehension accuracy is written as 0.86%, with a range of 0.66% to 0.98%. This is almost certainly intended to mean proportions or 86%, 66%, and 98%. As written, the values imply near-zero comprehension. Even if typographical, it is a reporting error in an important data-quality check.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%).

issues.description: Trials were visually inspected and excluded for incomplete reading or trace deviation, but the manuscript does not state whether the inspector was blind to condition or provide objective criteria. Unblinded subjective exclusions can bias eye-tracking results, particularly when effects are small.
issues.quote: All trials were also visually inspected in order to identify those where participants had not read the sentences in full, or where any considerable deviation in the eye-tracking trace was evident during the trial.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 3 text and table report different statistics
issues.description: The reported model estimates and test statistics for Experiment 3 differ between the Results text and Table 5. These inconsistencies make it unclear which model outputs are correct.
issues.quote: There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001) ... The effect of congruency on regressions-out was significant ... (B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01). ... Go-past time | ... | Estimate (B) | 43 | t = 3.76 *** ... Regressions-out | ... | Estimate (B) | 0.25 | z = 2.65 **

issues.description: Go-past times and fixation-duration measures are typically positively skewed. The manuscript reports linear mixed models on raw millisecond durations without reporting residual diagnostics, transformations, trimming beyond fixation-level cleaning, or robustness checks. Violations of model assumptions can affect standard errors and p-values.
issues.quote: We implemented linear mixed models or generalised linear models as appropriate ... Go-past time. This analysis considered the impact of congruency on the summed fixation duration (in ms)

issues.description: The entropy analysis concludes that spelling is more predictive than phonology because the slope of Hspelling regressed on Hphonology is less than 1. A regression slope is not an appropriate test of whether paired spelling entropies are lower than paired phonological entropies; it is affected by intercept, variance, measurement error, and regression-to-the-mean. A paired comparison or model of Hspelling - Hsound would be more direct. The reported mean difference is tiny and no paired test is reported.
issues.quote: We then examined the slope of the regression equation lm(Hspelling ~ Hphonology). ... a slope less than 1 would support our conjecture that spelling is more predictive of category compared to phonology.  We found that the regression line has a slope of 0.9 ... That is, the spellings of derivational suffixes generally yield better prediction of lexical category (mean H=0.61) than do their spoken realisations (mean H=0.63).

issues.subcategory: entropy values incompatible with stated category set
issues.description: The manuscript says the analyses consider three major lexical categories. If entropy is calculated over only nouns, adjectives, and verbs, the maximum possible entropy is log2(3) = 1.585. Appendix A reports entropy values above this, implying that additional categories were included or the calculation differs from the stated method. This inconsistency prevents interpretation of the entropy analysis.
issues.quote: Our analyses consider three major lexical categories: nouns, adjectives, and verbs. ... 132 | +st | ... | H phonology | 2.282 | H orthography | 2.295

issues.description: The discussion reports preliminary analyses that remove sets of suffixes after inspecting their diagnosticity/specificity and category relevance, including removing all suffixes with perfect values. These exclusions are not preregistered and use different criteria for different analyses, increasing researcher degrees of freedom in interpreting why some suffixes are diagnostic or specific.
issues.quote: For this analysis, we removed seven suffixes with diagnosticity below 0.35 ... Once we remove these 40 suffixes, a positive correlation is observed ... Similar dependency is characteristic of suffix specificity. As with the diagnosticity analyses, we excluded 20 suffixes with a low specificity in the type analysis ... We also removed all suffixes with the specificity of 1

issues.description: The manuscript makes causal and functional claims that English spelling evolved or became fractionated to maximize transmission of meaningful information. The presented evidence is cross-sectional corpus description plus behavioral sensitivity in modern readers. It does not establish diachronic causation, selection pressures, optimization, or that spelling-sound inconsistency exists in order to support spelling-meaning regularity.
issues.quote: We close by arguing that English spelling may have become fractionated in such a way that the high degree of spelling-sound inconsistency maximises the transmission of meaningful information. ... the results of our analyses suggest that the proliferation of spellings in English may actually be functional.

issues.subcategory: behavior interpreted as facilitation of meaning access
issues.description: The behavioral studies show classification choices, spelling choices, and eye-movement disruption under syntactic incongruency. They do not directly measure semantic access or demonstrate that suffix cues facilitate access to meaning. The causal mechanism is inferred rather than tested.
issues.quote: We have shown that the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction to do so (see our spelling and eye tracking data) suggesting that these cues facilitate access to meaning.

issues.subcategory: undergraduate sample generalized to average readers
issues.description: The manuscript generalizes from small samples of university undergraduates to "the average reader" and "literate adults." University students are not representative of the full population of skilled readers in age, education, literacy, dialect, or spelling experience. This overstates population generalizability.
issues.quote: We have shown that the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction to do so

issues.description: The manuscript speculates that diagnosticity and specificity reflect general cognitive principles that must appear in other orthographies, but no data from other writing systems are presented. The claim is only partially hedged and should be framed as a hypothesis.
issues.quote: It is our view that diagnosticity and specificity are characteristic not of the English writing system exclusively but rather reflect general cognitive principles and thus must manifest, in one way or another, in other orthographies.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent characterization of English spelling-sound regularity
issues.description: The General Discussion says English letters map relatively consistently to sounds, while much of the manuscript motivates the work by emphasizing English spelling-sound inconsistency and deep orthography. The inconsistency is not central to the analyses but weakens conceptual clarity.
issues.quote: English has an alphabetic writing system in which letters map relatively consistently to sounds. ... English is typically characterised as a deep orthography as a result of its high degree of inconsistency across this mapping

issues.subcategory: verb category not analyzed in eye-tracking despite broad claims
issues.description: Experiment 3 includes verb-suffix items only as fillers and excludes them from analysis because many verb suffixes are weakly diagnostic. Therefore the eye-tracking evidence primarily concerns noun/adjective suffixes, yet the conclusions are stated broadly for lexical category and skilled reading.
issues.quote: Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added so that sentence contexts would be balanced across all three lexical categories. These filler nonwords were not analysed, because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category
